o1.biggest_strength: It picks one clear move that targets the real problem in the data, and it correctly sees that the fastest two-quarter win must come from reducing churn and surfacing yearly billing rather than repricing the whole base.
o1.biggest_mistake: The revenue math and framing get a bit loose in places: some figures are slightly off or insufficiently explained, and it adds a second 'bolder move' after saying there should be one recommendation.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Tighten every number, keep to one recommendation only, and make the test and stop rule even cleaner by centering the decision on Essentials 8+ retention and Team cannibalization with no extra side proposal.

o2.biggest_strength: It is easy to read, sounds close to our brand, and stays focused on the highest-value segment problem: high-channel Essentials customers who hate per-channel creep and need approvals.
o2.biggest_mistake: It misses the bigger yearly-billing opportunity as part of the main recommendation and makes some assumptions and revenue claims that are too shaky for me to act on confidently, especially the price point and the month-6 math.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Use our data more fully by combining the flat plan with an honest yearly push, show more defensible math, and prove the proposed price and channel cap are the right tradeoff against Team downgrade risk.

reason: Output 1 understands my business case better and uses the constraints better, especially the two-quarter timing and the 12-month price promise. Output 2 is cleaner to read, but I would trust Output 1 more to guide a real pricing decision.
